topics.title: Average Flex
topics.description: Learn Solve Average Flex through focused explanations, worked examples, and practical binary-search problems.

pages.title: Average Flex
pages.content:
Averages can also be searched with binary search. For a candidate average `x`, subtract `x` from every element. The question becomes whether any length-K window has a transformed sum of at least zero.

If a feasible window exists, the true maximum average is at least `x`, so search higher. Otherwise search lower. This monotonic feasibility test allows binary search on a real-valued answer.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Average Flex highlights an important invariant, boundary, or complexity property of binary search.

checkpoint.question: What is the key idea in binary-searching an average?
options: Binary-search a candidate average and test whether a window can achieve at least that average.
Sort the array and always choose its first element.
Use a hash table to count every average.
Replace every element with its square.
checkpoint.explanation: Binary-search a candidate average and test whether a window can achieve at least that average.

pages.title: Elements less than or equal to Num
pages.content: If you have a sorted array $A_0 \leq A_1 \ldots \leq A_{n-1}$, how will you find the number of elements $\leq num$?

pages.title: Binary Search Student Scores
pages.content: If the number of students scoring less than or equal $A_i$ is $x$, what is the number of students scoring greater than $A_i$?

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary Search Student Scores highlights an important invariant, boundary, or complexity property of binary search.

pages.title: Prerequisite Check
pages.content: Before coding, identify what is ordered, what is monotonic, and what the candidate answer interval means. Write one sentence describing what remains possible.
pages.teachingGoal: State the prerequisite and the candidate search space.

pages.title: Core Intuition
pages.content: Binary search is not merely a loop template. It is a proof-driven elimination process: choose a midpoint, determine which side cannot contain the answer, and preserve the invariant on the remaining side.
pages.teachingGoal: Explain why one side can be discarded safely.

pages.title: Guided Dry Run
pages.content: Use the table **left | mid | right | test | decision | new interval**. Do not move a pointer until you can say why the discarded region is impossible.
pages.teachingGoal: Trace the algorithm without executing code.
pages.suggestedVisual: Annotated search interval shrinking around mid.

pages.title: Guided Implementation
pages.content: Write the boundary definitions first. Then write the loop and update rules. Finally run four tests: smallest input, exact boundary, missing answer, and largest relevant input.
pages.teachingGoal: Convert the invariant into safe Java 17 code.

pages.title: Mastery Gate
pages.content: You pass only when you can explain the invariant in plain language, reproduce the algorithm without copying, handle an edge case, and state time and space complexity.

practiceProblems.description: Given an array of positive integers and a required window length K, use binary search on the average to determine the maximum average of any length-K contiguous subarray.

topics.title: Coins and Triangle
topics.description: Learn Solve Coins and Triangle through focused explanations, worked examples, and practical binary-search problems.

pages.title: Coins And Triangle
pages.content:
A triangle of height `H` needs `H(H+1)/2` coins. As `H` increases, the required number of coins never decreases, so feasibility is monotonic.

Binary-search the largest feasible height:
- `H` is feasible when `H(H+1)/2 <= N`.
- If a midpoint is feasible, move right to try a larger height.
- Otherwise move left.

This is a classic example of binary search on the answer.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Coins And Triangle highlights an important invariant, boundary, or complexity property of binary search.

checkpoint.question: Why are lower and upper bounds useful in sorted arrays?
options: They locate the boundaries around a target, enabling insertion, counting, and range queries.
They always return the target value.
They require the array to be unsorted.
checkpoint.explanation: They locate the boundaries around a target, enabling insertion, counting, and range queries.

pages.title: Multiple Choice Question
pages.content:
For $r$ rows, we know that the number of coins needed is $1 + 2 + ... + r = r(r+1)/2$.

Let us call f(r) = $r(r+1)/2$.

So, if we have an infinite array whose elements are f(1), f(2), ..... , then we know that

- This array is increasing
- The answer is the last index such that f(r) = n. So we only need till n.

Also, we can use an implicit array, because we can find f(r) very quickly. So instead of having an array, we'll just have a function which returns f(r).

Now, how do we find the last index such that f(r) <= n?

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Multiple Choice Question highlights an important invariant, boundary, or complexity property of binary search.

practiceProblems.title: Lower Bound
practiceProblems.description: For a sorted array, find the first index whose value is greater than or equal to a target.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement lower bound with binary search and print the first index i such that arr[i] >= target. If no such index exists, print N.
constraints: Array is sorted in nondecreasing order.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Second line: N sorted integers. Third line: target.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Upper Bound in a Sorted Array
practiceProblems.description: For a sorted array, find the first index whose value is strictly greater than a target.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement upper bound with binary search and print the first index i such that arr[i] > target. If no such index exists, print N.
constraints: Array is sorted in nondecreasing order.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Second line: N sorted integers. Third line: target.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Find the Insert Position
practiceProblems.description: Given a sorted array and a target, find the index where the target should be inserted so the array remains sorted.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Return the first index where arr[i] >= target. This is the insertion position and is exactly the lower-bound index.
constraints: Array is sorted in nondecreasing order.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Second line: N sorted integers. Third line: target.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Floor and Ceil in a Sorted Array
practiceProblems.description: Find the floor and ceil of a target in a sorted array. Floor is the greatest value <= target; ceil is the smallest value >= target.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Use binary search to compute floor and ceil. Print `floor ceil`; print -1 when either value does not exist.
constraints: Array is sorted in nondecreasing order.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Second line: N sorted integers. Third line: target.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print two integers: floor and ceil, using -1 for a missing value.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: First and Last Occurrence
practiceProblems.description: In a sorted array, find the first and last index of a target using two binary searches.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Print the first and last 0-based positions of target. If target is absent, print `-1 -1`.
constraints: Array is sorted in nondecreasing order.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Second line: N sorted integers. Third line: target.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print first_index last_index, or -1 -1 when absent.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Perfect Root Finder
practiceProblems.description: Given a non-negative perfect square X, find its integer square root using binary search. Do not use floating-point square-root functions.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Find the integer r such that r*r = X. Inputs are guaranteed to be perfect squares.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Pyramid of Bricks
practiceProblems.description: A pyramid of height H requires 1+2+...+H bricks. Given N bricks, find the maximum complete height.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Print the greatest H such that H(H+1)/2 <= N.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print the maximum complete pyramid height.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.

practiceProblems.title: Coins And Triangle
practiceProblems.description: Given N coins, find the largest integer height H for which a complete triangle of H rows can be formed, requiring 1+2+...+H coins.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Find the largest H such that H(H+1)/2 <= N. Solve by binary search on H.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: One integer N, the number of coins.

practiceProblems.title: The Wave
practiceProblems.description: Given N distinct integers and K, find the smallest possible maximum distance from a chosen value to every selected element when selecting a contiguous block of K after sorting. This reduces to minimizing max-min over all length-K windows.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Sort the values, then find the minimum range (maximum - minimum) among every contiguous block of K values.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N K. Second line: N integers.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print the minimum possible range among K selected elements.
hints: Decide whether mid stays or is discarded.
